fields.explanation: A cryptographic hash maps any input to a fixed-size digest that is deterministic (the same input always gives the same digest) and one-way: there is no key and no inverse operation, so the input cannot be recovered from the digest. A different digest on each call is wrong too; if hashing were random it could not verify integrity or passwords.

A (req, res) function only works as a terminal handler that always responds, and Express never passes the app itself to middleware.

fields.explanation: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread and asks the operating system for non-blocking I/O; the event loop (libuv, using epoll, kqueue or IOCP) waits on many sockets at once and runs each callback when its data arrives, so thousands of connections overlap without a thread each. Thread-per-request is how classic servers such as Apache's worker MPM work, busy-polling would burn the CPU, and callbacks never get their own threads; only some file-system and crypto calls use a small libuv thread pool behind the scenes.

https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/cli.html UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE: 'Asynchronous system APIs are used by Node.js whenever possible, but where they do not exist, libuv's threadpool is used to create asynchronous node APIs based on synchronous system APIs.'
knowledge: Node 22 runs application JavaScript on one thread and drives socket I/O through libuv's non-blocking polling
